items.prompt: How does an animal work out which direction a sound came from?

options.label: It compares what each ear receives
options.feedback: Timing and loudness differ between the two.

options.label: It measures how loud the sound is
options.feedback: Loudness alone gives no direction.

options.label: It waits for the sound to repeat
options.feedback: One sound is enough to place a source.

options.label: It feels the sound through the ground
options.feedback: Some animals do, but that is not how ears work.

items.ok_line: Two ears, two slightly different reports, one direction.
items.ko_line: Ask why almost every animal has exactly two ears rather than one.
items.exp_title: Two ears, and the gap between them
items.exp_text: A sound from the left reaches the left ear a fraction earlier and slightly louder, since the head casts an acoustic shadow. The brain reads those differences — as little as ten millionths of a second in humans — and turns them into a direction. It is the same principle that gives two eyes their sense of depth, applied to sound, and it fails for sources directly in front or behind, which is why we tilt our heads.

items.prompt: Why is a barn owl's face shaped like a shallow dish?

options.label: It funnels sound towards the ears
options.feedback: The stiff feathers work as a collecting surface.

options.label: It keeps rain off the eyes
options.feedback: The shape works just as well in dry country.

options.label: It makes the bird look larger
options.feedback: The disc is not a display.

options.label: It shelters the beak while hunting
options.feedback: The beak needs no shelter.

items.ok_line: The whole face is an ear, and the eyes are only lodgers.
items.ko_line: The owl hunts in darkness. What might that face be collecting?
items.exp_title: A face built as an ear
items.exp_text: The barn owl's facial disc is a ring of stiff feathers that gathers sound and channels it to the ear openings hidden at its edges, working like a hand cupped behind the ear. It can adjust the shape of the disc by moving those feathers to focus better. Combined with ear openings set at different heights, it locates prey in both directions at once and strikes accurately in total darkness.

items.prompt: What makes an owl's flight almost silent?

options.label: Fringes along its wing feathers
options.feedback: They break up the turbulence that makes noise.

options.label: It glides without flapping
options.feedback: It flaps often, and still makes no sound.

options.label: It flies unusually slowly
options.feedback: Slow flight is noisy for most birds.

options.label: Its bones absorb the sound
options.feedback: The noise is made in the air, not the body.

items.ok_line: A comb along the leading edge, and velvet on top.
items.ko_line: Look closely at the front edge of an owl's wing. It is not smooth.
items.exp_title: A wing that refuses to whistle
items.exp_text: Flight noise comes from air tumbling off the wing. An owl's leading feathers carry a comb-like fringe that breaks the airflow into small eddies too quiet to hear, its trailing edge is ragged rather than sharp, and the upper surface is covered in velvety down that absorbs what remains. The silence serves twice: the mouse never hears it coming, and the owl can still hear the mouse.

items.prompt: How does a bat avoid deafening itself with its own calls?

options.label: A muscle shuts the ear as it calls
options.feedback: It closes on each shout and reopens for the echo.

options.label: It calls very quietly
options.feedback: Its calls are among the loudest sounds any animal makes.

options.label: It turns its head away when calling
options.feedback: The sound would reach its ears regardless.

options.label: Its ears cannot hear its own pitch
options.feedback: It must hear that pitch to read the echo.

items.ok_line: It closes its ears a hundred times a second, then opens them again.
items.ko_line: The call is deafeningly loud and the echo is faint. Something must protect the ear.
items.exp_text: A bat's calls can exceed 110 decibels at close range — as loud as a smoke alarm — while the returning echo is thousands of times fainter. A small muscle in the middle ear contracts a fraction before each call, damping the ear, and relaxes in time for the echo. It does this up to two hundred times a second, in precise step with the voice.

items.prompt: How does a dog find a trail hours after it was made?

options.label: It detects traces left on the ground
options.feedback: Skin cells and scent cling for hours.

options.label: It sees marks left in the grass
options.feedback: A dog tracks over bare stone as readily.

options.label: It hears the person still moving
options.feedback: The trail works long after anyone has gone.

options.label: It follows the warmth of footprints
options.feedback: Warmth fades within minutes.

items.ok_line: A trail is a chemical record, and it lasts.
items.ko_line: The person left hours ago. What could still be on the ground?
items.exp_text: We shed around forty thousand skin cells a minute, and each carries scent that clings to ground and vegetation. A dog's nose holds up to three hundred million receptors against our six million, and a far larger share of its brain is given to smell. It can even tell direction: by comparing the strength of scent between footprints a few paces apart, it works out which way the trail leads.

items.prompt: Why does a snake flick its tongue in and out?

options.label: To collect scent from the air
options.feedback: The forked tips deliver it to an organ in the roof of the mouth.

options.label: To taste what it is about to eat
options.feedback: Snakes swallow without tasting in that way.

options.label: To threaten whatever is nearby
options.feedback: It flicks constantly, threat or none.

options.label: To cool itself in warm weather
options.feedback: The tongue is far too small for cooling.

items.ok_line: It is sampling the air, and the fork tells it which way to go.
items.ko_line: Ask why the tongue is forked, and what it might be delivering.
items.exp_text: The tongue gathers scent particles and carries them to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of the mouth. Because it is forked, the two tips sample slightly separated points and the snake can tell which side carries more — smelling in stereo, exactly as two ears hear in stereo. That is how it follows a trail. It is not tasting, and the flicking has nothing to do with threat.

items.prompt: How do whiskers help an animal move in the dark?

options.label: They feel gaps and nearby surfaces
options.feedback: Each one reports the moment it bends.

options.label: They pick up scent from the air
options.feedback: Whiskers have no role in smell.

options.label: They sense warmth from ahead
options.feedback: They detect touch, not heat.

options.label: They keep the face clean
options.feedback: Grooming is done with tongue and paws.

items.ok_line: A map of the immediate surroundings, drawn by touch.
items.ko_line: A whisker is a hair rooted in nerves. What can it report?
items.exp_text: Each whisker sits in a follicle packed with nerve endings, reporting the slightest bend, and a cat can sweep them forward to feel ahead. They are roughly as wide as the body, so a gap the whiskers clear is a gap the animal fits through. Rats sweep theirs back and forth many times a second to build a picture of a burrow, and a seal's whiskers are sensitive enough to follow the wake a fish left thirty seconds earlier.

items.prompt: How does a mole find its way underground?

options.label: By touch and vibration
options.feedback: Its snout is among the most sensitive organs known.

options.label: By seeing in the dark
options.feedback: Its eyes are tiny and nearly useless.

options.label: By echoes off the tunnel walls
options.feedback: Moles do not use echolocation.

options.label: By remembering the whole tunnel
options.feedback: Memory helps, but it must sense new ground too.

items.ko_line: Underground there is no light and no room for echoes. What is left?
items.exp_title: A nose that reads the soil
items.exp_text: A mole's snout is covered in thousands of touch receptors called Eimer's organs, giving it a resolution of touch finer than a human fingertip. The star-nosed mole takes this furthest: its twenty-two fleshy rays sweep the ground and it identifies and eats prey in under a quarter of a second — the fastest feeding of any mammal recorded. It can also smell underwater, by blowing out bubbles and breathing them back in.

items.prompt: How does a shark detect a fish hidden under sand?

options.label: It senses the electricity of muscles
options.feedback: Pores on its snout pick up tiny electric fields.

options.label: It hears the fish breathing
options.feedback: The sound would not carry through sand.

options.label: It sees a shape through the sand
options.feedback: Sand blocks light completely.

options.label: It feels the sand shifting
options.feedback: A motionless buried fish shifts nothing.

items.ok_line: Every beating heart leaks a signal, and the shark reads it.
items.ko_line: The fish is buried and still. What can a living body not hide?
items.exp_text: A shark's snout is dotted with jelly-filled pores called the ampullae of Lorenzini, sensitive to electric fields of a few billionths of a volt per centimetre. Every contracting muscle and beating heart produces one, so a buried, motionless fish still announces itself. The same sense may help sharks navigate, since moving through Earth's magnetic field generates faint currents of its own.

items.prompt: Why can an elephant communicate with another many kilometres away?

options.label: It uses very low sounds
options.feedback: Low pitches travel far and bend around obstacles.

options.label: It uses very high sounds
options.feedback: High pitches fade within a short distance.

options.label: It signals by raising its trunk
options.feedback: Sight would not carry over that distance.

options.label: It leaves scent marks along the way
options.feedback: Scent works, but slowly and only on a trail.

items.ok_line: Below your hearing, and travelling for kilometres.
items.ko_line: Low sounds carry, high sounds fade. Which would you choose?
items.exp_text: Elephants produce rumbles down to about 14 hertz, below the human threshold. Low frequencies lose energy slowly and bend around obstacles, so the calls carry up to ten kilometres through forest and further at night when the air is still. Part of the sound travels through the ground as well, and elephants appear to detect it through their feet and trunk, sometimes freezing and pressing down to listen.
